Ugwu 5 min read · Just now -- Listen Share A Letter to the PM Just Starting Out Press enter or click to view image in full size Ai image created by Esther Onyinyechi Ugwu When I started in product management, I thought the job was about having great ideas. I pictured myself in a room, sketching features on a whiteboard while everyone nodded along. The reality was different. The job turned out to be less about ideas and more about judgement: knowing which problems matter, convincing people to work on them, and finding out quickly whether you were right. Nobody hands you a manual for that. You pick it up through mistakes, many of which I could have avoided. So if I could go back and start again, here are the seven things I would do differently, in order of how much I wish I had started sooner. 1. I would learn data analysis Press enter or click to view image in full size Ai photo generated by Esther Onyinyechi Ugwu This is the one I would start on day one. Early on, I relied on others to pull numbers for me. Every question meant a request, a wait, and a report that answered something slightly different from what I asked. I was making decisions on gut feeling and calling it product sense. Learning to work with data yourself changes everything. You stop guessing which feature people use and simply check. You spot the drop-off in your sign-up flow before anyone flags it. And in meetings, “I think” becomes “here’s what the numbers show”, which is a very different conversation. You don’t need to become a data scientist. Here is what I would focus on: Spreadsheets, properly. Pivot tables, lookups and simple charts will answer most of your questions. Basic SQL. Being able to write a simple query and pull your own data saves you days of waiting. Product metrics. Know the difference between activation, retention and engagement, and which ones matter for your product. Reading numbers critically. Ask what’s missing, what the sample size is, and whether a change is real or just noise. Data won’t make your decisions for you. But it will tell you when your instincts are wrong, and that is worth more than any idea 2. I would talk to users every single week Data tells you what is happening. Users tell you why. Early in my career, I talked to customers only when a project needed “validation”, which usually meant after the big decisions were already made. Now I would make it a habit: at least one or two conversations every week, no agenda except curiosity. Ask about their day, their frustrations, the workarounds they’ve invented. The best product ideas I’ve seen came from someone casually saying “oh, I just do this manually in Excel”. 3. I would learn to write clearly So much of a PM’s work is writing: specs, updates, proposals, messages to stakeholders. A clear one-page document can align a whole team. A messy one creates a week of confusion and three extra meetings. I would practise writing short. Lead with the point. Cut the jargon. Before sending anything, I would ask: if someone reads only the first two lines, will they know what I need from them? 4. I would understand the technology I don’t mean learning to code like an engineer. I mean understanding enough to ask good questions: how an API works, what a database does, why something “small” might actually take three weeks. When you understand the basics, engineers stop translating everything for you, your estimates get more realistic, and you earn a level of respect that no amount of enthusiasm can buy. 5. I would learn how the business makes money For a long time I focused only on users and features. I didn’t really understand pricing, margins, customer acquisition costs or why leadership kept talking about revenue targets. That was a mistake. A great product that doesn’t support the business won’t survive. When you understand how money flows through the company, your priorities sharpen and your proposals start landing with leadership, because you’re speaking their language. 6. I would get comfortable saying no As a new PM, I wanted everyone to be happy. Sales wanted a feature, support wanted a fix, the CEO had an idea over the weekend, and I tried to fit it all in. The result was a roadmap that did many things poorly. The real job is choosing. Every “yes” is a “no” to something else. I would learn to say no kindly but clearly, explain the trade-off, and point back to the goal everyone agreed on. 7. I would invest in my engineers and designers Press enter or click to view image in full size Ai photo generated by Esther Onyinyechi Ugwu Your team doesn’t work for you; you work with them. I would spend more time understanding how they think, involving them early in problems instead of handing them finished solutions, and giving them credit loudly when things go well. The best products I’ve seen were built by teams that trusted each other. That trust is built in small moments, long before the big launch. You don’t need all of this on day one Press enter or click to view image in full size Ai photo generated by Esther Onyinyechi Ugwu If this list feels like a lot, that’s because it is. Nobody masters all seven in their first year, and that’s fine. Product management is a craft you grow into, one project and one mistake at a time.
